content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Explain why equations must be balanced
Write balanced symbol equations from word equations
Check that equations are correctly balanced
to show conservation of mass. A balanced equation has the same number of atoms of each element on both sides of the arrow.
Explore equation balancing — practise balancing chemical equations by adjusting coefficients using the interactive visualisation below.
- no atoms are created or destroyed
- same total mass before and after
- we need correct ratios for calculations
Start with elements that appear in only one place on each side
Balance metals first, then non-metals, then hydrogen, then oxygen
Check all atoms balance at the end
Balance oxygen by putting 2 in front of H₂O
Balance hydrogen by putting 2 in front of H₂
Balance Fe: put 2 in front of Fe
Balance O: 3 on left, 2 on right. LCM = 6
Need 3 CO₂ to give 6 O on right
Balance C: 1 on left, 3 on right
Balance: C₃H₈ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O (combustion of propane)
Balance C: put 3 in front of CO₂
Balance H: 8 on left, put 4 in front of H₂O
Count O on right: (3 × 2) + 4 = 10 oxygen atoms Need 10 O atoms on left: put 5 in front of O₂
This is tricky because of the bracket. Al₂(SO₄)₃ contains: 2 Al, 3 S, 12 O
Balance Al: put 2 in front of Al
Balance S: 1 on left, 3 on right. Put 3 in front of H₂SO₄
Balance H: 6 on left (3 × 2). Put 3 in front of H₂
Add state symbols to show physical states:
Only change the big numbers in front of formulas
Always check ALL elements are balanced at the end
Use whole numbers only (multiply everything if needed)
Equations must be balanced to show conservation of atoms/mass
Only change coefficients (big numbers), never subscripts
Count atoms of each element on both sides
Balance one element at a time
Check all elements at the end
Common order: metals, then non-metals, then H, then O
